1 Introduction 
1.1 Overview 
Welcome to PDView3 TM. This software package complements and enhances Iris 
Power’s PDA-IV Lite™, TGA-B Lite™, TGA-S Lite™, HydroGuardTM, TurboGuardTM, 
BusGuardTM, HydroTracTM, BusTracTM and PDTracTM systems (hereafter referred to 
collectively as Iris instruments)1, in their ability to measure partial discharge activity 
in motors, generators, switchgear and air-cored transformers. 
With PDView3 test results from your in strument can be displayed and interpreted 
through the use of various graphical reports. There are three levels of user 
interface: Simple, Standard, and Advanced modes. You do not have to be an 
expert to produce quality reports, though a basic understanding of partial discharge 
(PD) theory and the Microsoft ® Windows 2 environment is assumed. For further 
information regarding PD theory contact Iris Power, for further information 
regarding Microsoft® Windows refer to the Microsoft® Windows User’s Guide. 
PDView3 offers a great deal of flexibility and creativity for those who like to 
experiment or prefer to use their ow n customized formats; however, this 
customization section of the software, referred to as Advanced mode, does require 
a special software release. Both the Simple and Standard modes are designed for 
easy, user-friendly interface that should meet the majority of your needs, and are 
provided upon request. Should you be in doubt as to what your data acquisition 
needs are, please contact your sales representative at Iris Power, 
marketing@irispower.com. 
Changes to periodic testing instruments and the addition of continuous stator 
winding monitors, portable rotor winding monitors and monitors for other electrical 
equipment such as transformers and switchgear, as well as the integration of these 
into local plant systems have resulted in increased requirements for a new 
database design. The Iris Instrumentation Database (IID) design was developed to 
meet all of these needs. The IID design constitutes a unified database for all 
instruments of Iris Power.

For users of previous data acquisition software, PDLite, who want to 
use PDView3, your data from the older Paradox ®3 structure must 
be converted to the IID format. Data collected with PDLitePro or 
PDTracPro will not need to be converted. Data collected with 
HydroTracs, BusTracs, TurboGuards, HydroGuards and BusGuards 
must also be converted before using PDView3. [See Section 1.2.2]. 
Although we have made every attempt to ensure PDView3 is bug free, should you 
encounter difficulties with this software or have suggestions for improvement, 
please refer to the Customer Support Section 12.1 of this document. Once you 
have installed the PDView3 application on your computer, take the time to read this 
document to ensure you are familiar with the features needed to use your Iris 
instrument. 
1.2 Features 
PDView3 is a very powerful graphical display processor when compared to 
previous versions of PDView and AdvanceView. Some of the differences include: 
• Greatly expanded and improved graphing options including creation of 
customized templates 
• Ability to save data with reports into documents that can be opened later or 
transmitted without the need to open the database 
• Ability to select and display test results collected over time from the same 
equipment using different data collection devices 
1.2.1 User Modes 
PDView3 constitutes the new viewer for PD data acquired by any of Iris 
instruments. The viewer has a simple, user-friendly interface while incorporating 
advanced viewing features. 
Since users of PD technology have different requirements for the functionality 
embedded in PDView3, there are three different user-interfaces of varying 
complexity. The user interfaces are: Simple Mode, Standard Mode and Advanced 
Mode. 
1.2.1.1 Simple Mode 
Simple Mode corresponds to the functionality embedded in the older PDView2 ™ 
software. Simple Mode allows for viewing and printing of trend plots as well as 
Pulse Height Analysis Plots (2D Plot) and Pulse Phase Analysis Plots (3D plots). 
The features of Simple Mode are described in detail in section 6 of this manual. 
1.2.1.2 Standard mode 
Standard Mode corresponds to the functionality embedded in the older 
AdvanceView™ software. New functionality is introduced by providing pre-defined 
templates for PD data acquired via the portable instruments: TGA/PDA-IV and the 
continuous monitoring systems: Guards and Tracs. Furthermore, PD reports may 
be saved as a PDView documents containing the report formatting as well as the

1.2.1.3 Advanced Mode 
Advanced Mode contains complex functionality while maintaining the simple and 
user-friendly interface of Standard Mode. Examples are report manipulation, 
definition of custom report templates, and the display of Advanced Summary 
Numbers such as mode, mean, standard deviation, skew and kurtosis for 
fundamental PD Counters. The features of Advanced Mode are described in detail 
in section 8 of this manual. 
1.2.2 DataConverter 2.3 
Iris Power has developed a database converter – DataConverter 2.3, to enable 
users of Iris technology who have PD data stored in the older Paradox based 
databases to assess insulation degradation via PDView3 using the new Iris 
Instrument Database (IID) format. 
When using PDView3 in conjunction with data from PDLite, TracCon or 
PDGuardPro, and thus the older Paradox ® database design, a conversion is 
necessary each time newly acquired data is to be viewed in PDView3. The 
conversion process may be lengthy depending on the size of the Paradox 
database and the processing power of the computer on which the conversion takes 
place. The new application software for portable instruments, PDLitePro, as well as 
the application software for PDTrac instruments work with the new IID design; thus, 
there is full compatibility between PDLitePro, PDTracPro and PDView3. [See 
Section 9]

2.2 Quick Start 
 
Five Easy Steps: 
Install Software 
! Insert the auto start CD ROM in your drive. Follow the install wizard 
instructions. This will install PDView3 and DataConverter 2.3. 
! Run PDView3 or DataConverter 2.3 by accessing the Iris folder under 
Programs$Iris in your Microsoft Windows Start menu. DataConverter 
2.3 will allow you to convert Paradox based databases into the new Iris 
Instrument Database (IID), while PDView3 will allow you to create reports 
and interpretative graphs of your PD data. 
 
Convert Database (if required) 
! If you currently have any Iris databases in the Paradox ®-based .zip 
format, you are required to convert them to the new IID format in order to 
use PDView3. PDTrac and PDLitePro users do not need to convert data. 
! Run DataConverter 2.3, click the “Conversion Wizard” button and follow 
the instructions. The database converter can convert either a zipped 
database or a database directory into the new IID format. 
Note: DataConverter 2.3 can also be accessed in the PDView3 interface 
by selecting the Database Converter command in the Tools Menu 
(Tools$Database Converter) . For more detailed information, please 
refer to Section 9 of the PDView3 Help Document. 
 
Open Database 
! Now that your database is in the new IID format, you may proceed to 
opening your database in PDView3. 
! Under the File Menu, select the Open Database command (File $ Open 
Database). Select the IID file that you wish to open by browsing in the 
appropriate file folder window. 
! Upon opening a database file, you will immediately see information in the 
lower-left corner of the PDView3 screen. This screen is referred to as the 
Database Window.

3.3 Scroll bars 
The scroll bars appear whenever you may need to view work that is larger than 
your work window. The scroll bar along the right side allows you to move the 
screen up or down, while the scroll bar along the bottom allows you to move the 
screen left or right. You will only see the scroll bars when they are necessary. 
Work windows may also be resized to suit personal preferences by simply moving 
the window splitter bars. 
For Pulse Phase Analysis 3D plots, scroll bars to change the graph orientation will 
appear when the window is activated for editing (double-click). In zoom mode for 
Trend plots, the scroll bars can be used to scroll through the data. 
3.4 Menu Commands 
Commands are grouped in menus and can be accessed via the menu bar across 
the top of the main screen. The menu bar changes or is inactivated (dimmed) 
based on the applicability to your current action. When you select a menu item 
that is followed by an arrow ( !), a sub-menu is displayed from which you must 
make another choice. In this manual, main menu items appears as File and sub-
menus as File $ Open Database, with Open Database being the sub-menu. 
Several functions are accessible via right-click pop-up menus. In this manual, 
these items appear as % Hide Folder . Right-click pop-up menus are context-
menu sensitive, so their options change based on the current action. Some menu 
items are accessible through tool bar icons [see Section 4.1.4.3] and/or accelerator 
(hot) keys [see Section 11]. 
Menus can be opened from any page by using the <Alt> key along with the 
underscored letter specific for each menu. Once the menus are open, an option 
can be selected by pressing the underscored letter for that option.

Although all of your data is saved immediately into the open Database,

Reload is necessary if another application process is also putting data into or 
changing the database at the same time. For example, if you are using 
PDLitePro to view data and have changed the operating conditions or comments, 
it is necessary to reload the database in order to see the changes in PDView3. 
You can do this by File $ Reload Database.

4.2.2.1 Editing Graph objects 
Graph objects have three states: Non-active, Active and Editable. 
When a graph is Non-active, PD data may not be linked or dragged to it for 
display, nor may the graph object be manipulated for appearance or data display 
parameters. An example of a non-active graph object is given in Figure 4-1 (left). 
When a graph object is Active, it may be resized and/or moved within the Report 
Window, and PD data may be linked or dragged to it for display. However, the 
graph object may not be edited for appearance or data display parameters.

When a graph is Editable, the graph may be edited for appearance as well as

There are some terms used throughout this manual that are technical or

5.1 Measurement Criteria 
5.1.1 Phases 
For each graph object, graph type or text box, you have a choice of which phase or

5.1.4 Reference Angle 
In order to properly calibrate the Iris instrument, the phase shift between the power 
frequency reference voltage and the voltage of the phase being tested must be 
determined. For all installations using capacitive couplers, this angle is 90 °. For 
installations with stator slot couplers (SSCs), the reference angle is based on the

5.2 Pulse Categories (counters) 
In the majority of cases, the graphs show the partial discharge counts or categories 
versus some condition, such as magnitude, ac phase angle, or time. Often more 
than one pulse category can be plotted on the same graph, creating a family of 
curves (see Sections 7.2 and 7.3.3). 
5.2.1 Directly Measured Pulse Categories 
When the IRIS instrument measures the pulse signals from a sensor, it categorizes 
the pulses according to polarity (positive or negative), where the partial discharge 
may have originated (near coupler C1 or C2 with the PDA-IV Lite, HydroGuard and 
HydroTrac, from the unit or Bus with a TGA-B, BusGuard and BusTrac, and from 
the endwinding or slot with the TGA-S and TurboGuard using SSCs) or whether 
the pulse is due to noise from outside of the winding. A pulse counter in the test 
instrument is assigned to each of these fundamental categories or types of pulses. 
Tables 5.1 to 5.3 show the fundamental (or directly measured) pulse categories for 
each type of sensor. This raw data can be exported to a .csv file or viewed as 
described in Section 7.4 and Section 7.4.2, respectively. 
5.2.2 Derived Pulse Categories 
In addition to the fundamental pulse categories, two kinds of data are derived. The 
first is a simple combination of two or more fundamental pulse categories, such as 
“Slot Total” in Table 5.4 and “Total System Noise” in Table 5.5. Whereas the 
second type is a single quantity, which can summarize all the test results from a 
single test, called a PD activity indicator or summary number (see Section 5.2.3). 
Some of the derived pulse categories are just simple additions of the fundamental 
pulse categories and/or derived categories. However, two special pulse category 
types have also been created: bipolar and absolute. The bipolar category plots 
positive pulses on the positive scale and negative pulses on the negative scale, as 
in Linear Density Plots [Figure 5-4]. In contrast, the absolute category ignores the 
polarity of the pulses and plots both positive and negative pulses on the positive 
scale, as in Polar Plots [Figure 5-5] and Pulse Phase Analysis Plots – 3D [Figure

5.2.3 PD Activity Indicators (NQN and Qm) 
The Iris instruments calculate the quantities Q m and NQN based on the entire 
Pulse Height Analysis (PHA) plot (see Section 5.3). The NQN, or Normalized 
Quantity Number, is a partial discharge quantity that is proportional to the total 
partial discharge measured by a PD sensor . The negative NQN refers to the total 
activity from negative PD pulses, while positive NQN refers to the total PD activity 
from positive PD pulses. NQN is an indi cator of the average condition of the stator 
winding insulation. 
Qm, or Peak Magnitude, is the magnitude of the pulses for one fundamental 
(directory measured) pulse category that has a repetition rate of 10 pulses per 
second, and corresponds to the peak PD activity. Q m is an indicator of how severe 
the PD is at the most deteriorated part of the winding. Positive and negative Q m 
refers to the peak PD activity from the positive and negative PD pulses, 
respectively. See your instrument manual for more information. 
For our purposes, Qm and NQN are derived from the basic test result data and are 
valuable for comparisons amongst machines or trending over time.

5.3.4 Pulse Density Linear Plot 
The Pulse Density Linear Plot graph type 
– often referred to as the linear pulse 
density plot – is perhaps one of the most 
used graph types for display of partial 
discharge data [Figure 5-4]. This two 
dimensional plot displays the partial 
discharge activity as a function of phase 
angle. A color-coding provides 
information on the pulse repetition rate for 
a given combination of phase-angle and 
magnitude. 
Please note that the major unit division of 
the pulse phase scale (the x-axis) is 45 ° 
and the minor unit division is 15 °. This 
allows for quick identification of the phase angle value at which a given PD cluster 
is centered. Specifically, this allows for quick discrimination between slot and 
interphasal partial discharge sources, as shown with the interphasal activity in 
Figure 5-4. 
The PPA Standard PD Report contains six gr aphs, specifically six Linear Pulse 
Density Plots, organized in three rows, one per phase. The data can be displayed 
in Standard form, where all three phases are shown relative to their respective 
phase-to-ground voltages. Or, the data can be displayed shifted, where the first 
row of graphs displays data measured on one phase with no phase shift. The 
second row of graphs displays data measured on the second phase but with the 
phase-angle scale shifted 120 ° from the first phase. The third row of graphs 
displays data measured on the third phase shifted 240 ° from the first phase. Thus, 
the sinusoidal phase voltages are displayed as they occur simultaneously in time. 
This allows for identification of phase-to-phase dependent discharge sources and 
cross-coupled PD clusters. Pulses from the same source, such as interphasal 
arcing or cross coupling will vertically ali gn. This data is not available from Trac 
instruments.

making it easy to determine whether the PD

5.5 Scaling & Units 
5.5.1 Relevance 
5.5.1.1 External Attenuators 
In many cases, more and more each day, due to the extremely high PD activity, it is 
necessary to use an external attenuator during data collection. This test setup requires 
that the values stored in the database be scaled up to the original values. During data 
collection a “scaling” factor based on the value of the attenuator was entered with the 
test measurement. 
5.5.1.2 Off-line Testing 
According to IEC 60034-27, Clause 8, when doing off-line testing it is essential to 
normalize the mV results to a pC level for trending and comparison to similar machines. 
The recommended normalization technique is to be used for each test setup and each 
phase, and is to be repeated during each testing cycle. 
5.5.2 Scaling 
In the Database ⇒ Measurement Window the scale factor is displayed. Note that a 
value of 1.00 means there is no scaling, whereas, a number less than 1.00 means the 
values will be scaled downwards and a number greater than 1.00 means the values will 
be scaled upwards. 
 
 
 
Figure 7. Scaling Factor 
 
Numbers that will be scaled are the sensitivity range and peak magnitudes ( ±Qm). As 
the Normalized Quantity Number ( ±NQN) has no meaning when scaled, these will be 
marked as Not Applicable (NA). 
In addition, if the scale factor is not equal to 1.00, for each of the graph plots, the axes 
will be appropriately adjusted and the magnitude axis title will reflect the applied scaling 
factor. 
Note: When data is exported as described in Section 4.1.1.6, the data is 
scaled, but Raw data as described in Section 7.4 is not.

7 Standard Mode Functionality 
Standard mode has a user-friendly interface maintaining a simple and intuitive 
interface structure. This user interface was designed to allow you to select data, 
create a PD report and print a graph using a minimum of operations. In the 
following sections, the basic functionality embedded in PDView3 allowing for quick 
creation of PD reports will be discussed, as well as more complicated functions 
allowing for rudimentary data manipulation. For instance, 
• Pre-defined templates allows for quick definition of phase-shifted Linear 
Pulse Density Plots for identification of interphasal PD sources as well as 
cross-coupled PD. 
• PD reports may be saved as documents containing not only the report 
formatting but also the raw PD data sets used in the report. A saved PD 
report may be opened in PDView3 on a later date and manipulated without 
opening the source database. 
• Direct e-mailing of reports to Iris Power for further analysis. 
• Rudimentary data manipulation including creation of custom PD counters. 
• Export of Raw Data to a .csv file pre-formatted for quick data manipulation in 
external application software. 
• Export of individual graphs and plots to image files or the clipboard for use in 
other documents. 
• Export of entire PD reports as image files for use in presentation and 
documents. 
 
Unlike Advanced Mode, Standard Mode does not allow for custom 
templates to be created or changes to templates to be saved. However, 
in Standard Mode any changes to a graph format will be saved with the 
data when a report document is saved.

9 Interpretation 
The download and analysis of collected data should be repeated at least every six 
months for machines rated 6kV and up. If a problem develops, then the frequency 
of collection may need to be increased. Due to the short-time frame between 
detection and failure for motors rated less than 6kV, it is recommended that 
analysis be done monthly on these machines. By using the summary archive 
variables, trending of data is straightforward and useful. Collection of data at 
different operating parameters using PDLitePro may also help in determining the 
condition of the stator winding. 
9.1 Trend Analysis 
The first step of analysis is to compare the results of the current test with any 
previous test results. If the unit operating parameters – voltage, load, winding 
temperature and gas pressure – are similar to those of the previous test, then a 
direct comparison can be made between the two test results. For cases where the 
operating parameters are not the same, refer to Sections 9.3.4-9.3.7. In order to 
compare tests it is best to collect data at operating conditions within certain ranges, 
such as:

can lead to fluctuations in PD levels

then it is likely the PD levels will change with load.

internal voids, which affects PD magnitudes.

the endwinding or ring busses 
Environmental conditions such as humidity may have a very noticeable impact, 
especially if the surface contamination becomes partly conductive when damp, so 
it should be recorded from one test to the next. It is appreciated that at times it 
may be very difficult to duplicate test conditions, particularly temperatures; 
however, the emphasis should always be on trying to achieve as uniform 
conditions as possible. This generally means taking tests when units are hot and 
the temperature has stabilized. When unloading a machine to do a reduced or no 
load test, it is inevitable the temperature will be in a state of transition through the 
test. In these cases, it is important to quickly conduct the tests to minimize the 
effects of temperature differences. Depending on the rate of temperature change, 
tests using the 1-second option may be warranted.

sections.heading: Halaman 81: PDView Help Manual Interpretation • 9-2
sections.content:
Iris Power 
When a trend line is established for PD tests taken over a period, it will be obvious 
that most show an up and down variation between successive tests. However, as 
an insulation system ages, there will be a discernible overall upward movement of 
PD with time. Aging is a very slow process and sudden increases are not 
expected in the PD test results. A doubling of PD activity (Qm values twice that of 
the previous test) every six months is a strong indication of a rapidly developing 
failure mechanism. Though the condition of the stator winding can be assessed, 
time to failure cannot be predicted. The actual failure is normally the result of an 
unusual source of insulation stress such as lightning, out-of-phase synchronization, 
or severe overheating. 
Caution: Erratic PD can cause wide swings in trends that may be 
misleading. Do not interpret these in isolation. 
Maintenance can often be done on a machine to lower the PD activity. Examples 
of maintenance that have been known to successfully reduce PD are rewedging, 
cleaning, dipping and baking, and repairs to the voltage stress coatings. If the 
source of the PD is within the bulk of the insulation, then repairs may not be 
effective. 
9.2 Comparison to Similar Machines 
As mentioned in Section 9.1, data collected from the same 
machine operating under similar parameters using the same 
test setup are directly comparable and the most useful. It is 
also possible to roughly compare the results of one machine to 
those of similar machines. Due to the influence of the test 
frequency on the results, the test setup (sensors and Iris 
instrument) must be the same for all comparisons. Based on 
statistical analysis, the type of machine does not appear to 
have a great impact on PD levels and though insulation types 
have different types of failure mechanisms, in these gross 
comparisons there does not appear to be much difference in the overall levels of 
PD activity. Load and temperature can also greatly influence test results, but these 
are dependent upon the type and condition of the insulation system, and thus, 
cannot be used in these gross comparisons. The remaining operating variables – 
voltage and gas coolant – must be similar to compare results. 
Statistical summaries of the Qm values based on the Iris database containing over 
80,000 test results as of 2006 are available on the Iris website. Data are separated 
by sensor, gas coolant, and voltage class. All of the data was acquired using an 
Iris test instrument: a Trac or Guard continuous monitor system, or a portable TGA, 
PDA-IV instrument. Each table shows the average, maximum, and the 25 th, 50th, 
75th, 90th, and 95 th percentile ranks. The 25 th percentile is the Qm magnitude for 
which 25% of the test results are below and are too small to interpret, similarly for 
50%, 75%, 90%, and 95%. Normally, there is concern for a winding if the Qm in a 
machine is higher than the 90th percentile and increasing.

sections.content:
Iris Power 
9.3 PD Characteristics 
9.3.1 Comparison Between Phases 
When the PD levels and patterns are similar among the phases, then uniform 
deterioration is suspected; otherwise, an isolated problem is more likely. Typically, 
coil looseness, thermal deterioration, contamination, and problems with the voltage 
stress coatings are widespread, or uniform, whereas, improper manufacturing and 
inadequate spacing are often isolated problems. 
9.3.2 Pulse Distribution 
The pulse distribution with respect to the AC phase position in 
the 3D plots can assist in determining the source of any problems 
in the stator winding. Normal, or classic, pulse distributions are 
Gaussian, with a mean of 45 ° for negative pulses, 225 ° for 
positive pulses and a standard deviation of 15 °, and are 
indicative of spherical shaped voids within the slot section of the 
core. Classic pulses are phase-to-ground voltage dependent. 
Narrow band pulses usually originate from PD occurring at sharp 
metallic corners, such as connections. Wide band pulses may 
indicate multiple failure mechanisms or perhaps elongated 
voids. PD patterns scattered across the ac cycle suggests 
either contamination, noise, or perhaps a combination of 
several failure mechanisms occurring simultaneously. If the 
PD is evenly distributed across the ac cycle, usually in 
distinguishable streams, often 6 in number, then the source of 
the pulses is typically from static excitation systems and not 
indicative of a problem with the winding. Void shapes are 
rarely standard and often result in unusual patterns that cannot be easily 
described. One example of unusual patterns is when the PD is skewed, non-
Gaussian, because of space charge effects within the voids. 
9.3.3 Polarity Predominance 
The polarity of the classic pulses and their 
predominance tells a lot about the 
dominant failure mechanism as shown in 
Figure 9-1. Due to space charge effects, a 
pulse will occur in a specific direction based 
on the proximity of the void to a metallic 
substance. For this reason, it is possible to 
determine where the pulses originate, and 
therefore, the location of the voids in the 
insulation system. Positive predominance 
is an indicator of surface activity, whereas 
negative predominance indicates voids 
near the conductor surface. No polarity 
predominance is most often indicative of 
voids within the bulk of the groundwall 
insulation. Several failure mechanisms can produce voids predominantly at a 
certain location in the insulation. Note that polarity predominance should be based

sections.content:

only on the classic PD patterns, and in the absence of classic PD, polarity 
predominance is not applicable (Section 9.3.2). 
9.3.4 Load Effect 
If tests are taken at loads that differ by at least 40%, it may be possible to ascertain 
the effects of magnetic forces on coil vibration. For loose windings, classic PD can 
be extremely load-dependent with positive PD activity increasing with the load. 
This is due to the increase in magnetic forces (F m ∝ I2) causing an increase in coil 
movement and thus surface (positive) PD activity. The effect is most significant 
with loose thermoset (hard) windings such as epoxy-mica insulated windings. 
Thermoplastic (soft) windings expand when heated and tend to secure themselves 
within the core. If PD load dependency is observed, it is always a concern that 
loose coils can lead to premature winding failure. These coil movements can 
rapidly damage the semi-conducting coating on the coil side and, if left unchecked, 
can wear away the insulation itself. In extreme cases, this failure mechanism can 
destroy an otherwise good winding in only a few years. 
9.3.5 Temperature Effect 
Operating temperature can greatly affect t he results from a partial discharge test. 
Various materials respond differently to changes in temperature. These changes 
can be subtle for small variances of +/-5 °C, or drastic, doubling and tripling, for 
greater discrepancies of +/-20 °C. Performing the PD test with the machine at the 
same load, but at different temperatures, i.e. at least +/-20 °C may be able to help 
further identify which failure mechanisms are occurring. These are often referred 
to as “Cold” and “Hot” tests. 
The sizes of voids within a stator winding are usually inversely proportional to the 
operating temperature. As temperature increases, the copper and groundwall 
bonding material expand closing voids and thus decreasing classic PD. This 
negative temperature effect is most significant on asphalt and polyester windings, 
but can also be observed on epoxy windings. A large negative temperature effect 
suggests more severe internal delamination. Note that RTD temperatures taken 
outside of the groundwall insulation do not quickly reflect changes in the 
temperature of the copper conductor or internal insulation. 
It may be found that the positive classic PD actually increases with temperature, a 
positive temperature effect . This phenomenon is frequently an indication of 
deterioration of the semicon/grading coating. As the temperature of the stator 
winding increases, the resistance of the coatings decreases and results in an 
increase in surface (positive) PD activity . This problem is generally a very slow 
failure mechanism, but often leads to high ozone production in air-cooled 
machines. 
9.3.6 Hydrogen Pressure Effect 
Since the occurrence of a partial discharge is greatly affected by the void shape 
and gas pressure within the void, variances in operating hydrogen pressure can 
lead to high fluctuations of the overa ll PD activity. These changes can be subtle, 
for small variances of +/-2 psi, or drastic, doubling and tripling, for greater 
discrepancies of +/-5psi. Performing the PD test with the machine at the same 
load, but at different operating pressures, i.e. at least +/-10psi, may be able to help

sections.heading: Halaman 84: PDView Help Manual Interpretation • 9-5
sections.content:
Iris Power 
identify which failure mechanisms are occurring. If the PD decreases with small 
increases in the hydrogen pressure ( negative effect), then the sources of PD are 
most likely within the hydrogen environment. If there is no noticeable change in 
the PD pattern at different hydrogen pressures (none) or a decrease in PD at lower 
pressure ( positive effect) , then it is likely the PD is from sources external to the 
hydrogen environment at the machine’s terminals. Note this final statement only 
applies to Bus installs on hydrogen-cooled machines, not for SSC applications. 
9.3.7 Humidity Effect 
Perhaps the most influential, yet unpredictable, impacts of ambient conditions to 
PD are the effects of variances in ambient humidity on air-cooled machines. 
Humidity can cause the electrical breakdown stress of the air to decrease, and 
therefore cause an increase in surface PD. Humidity can affect the electrical 
tracking of surface PD, and therefore cause a decrease in PD. Thus, in some 
circumstances, the PD may go up, while in others it would go down with increases 
in relative humidity. In some circumstances, the humidity effect has been known to 
cause the PD to fluctuate by as much as 300%. Since each scenario is different, it 
is extremely important the ambient humidity be recorded at test time so trends can 
be properly evaluated and decisions are not made about upward trends that occur 
because of humidity effects and not changes in winding condition. Present 
experience indicates humidity only affects surface activity.

PDTracPro™ A software package that controls the PDTrac instrument 
Phase rotation The relationship between the three phases within the winding based 
on the rotation and nomenclature of the machine, either ABC or ACB 
Phase-shift 
When PD is displayed phase-shifted from the standard 0 ° - 360 ° 
representation, usually done based on the phase rotation of the 
winding 
Polar pulse plot 
A graph type that is a two-dimensional phase-resolved plots 
comparing absolute PD magnitude versus the polar representation of 
the phase-to-ground voltage reference 
Pulse height plot – 
2D

versus the pulse repetition rate in pulses per second 
Pulse phase plot – 
3D

Iris Power 
Qm Peak PD magnitude in mV at 10 pps 
Raw data 
The actual pulse counts that are separated based on polarity, pulse 
classification, and occurrence relative to the phase-to-ground voltage 
reference 
Report A combination of graphs and text boxes that have been formatted and 
had data attached 
Scaling factor 
For use when on-line testing is done with external attenuators or off-
line tests need to be normalized. Ranges, plots and peak magnitudes 
(Qm) will be adjusted appropriately. NQN are not scaled. 
Single-ended install When only one coupler is connected per phase 
Slot discharges Discharges that occur between the surface of the coil and the core 
Slot portion The portion of the coil/bar located within the stator core section 
Stator slot couplers 
(SSC) 
High-frequency antennae that detect high-frequency PD signals 
Template A combination of graph objects that have been formatted without data 
attached that are saved for future use 
Test data set A single test result collected using one of the Iris instruments 
Test ranges The test sensitivity used by the Iris instrument when PD data was 
collected 
Text box A graph object that allows the user to select Text parameters to 
display with a report for descriptive identification 
TGA™ 
Turbine Generator Analyzer – a portable test instrument for 
monitoring PD activity in turbine generators and motors that acquires 
phase-resolved PD using a directional time-of-arrival noise 
identification technique 
TGA-B™ A TGA instrument used to measure PD collected on a BUS Install 
TGA-S™ A TGA instrument used to measure PD on a machine with SSC 
sensors 
Time-of-arrival 
A noise identification technique that compares the arrival of pulses 
from two different couplers to determine the direction of the PD 
source 
Trend Analysis A graph type that compares NQN and Q m values collected at different 
times 
TurboGuard 
A permanently mounted instrument that continuously collects PD data 
activity on turbine generators with SSCs based on triggers set 
according to the operating parameters inputs
